protocol.task: Evaluate extraction against source; gold is optional annotation, never candidate instructions.

dimensions.completeness: Meaningful article coverage, including headings, lists, code and notes. Do not demand navigation.
dimensions.cleanliness: Exclude navigation, ads, feedback, recommendations, duplicates. Legitimate editorial links remain. Cite s:N noise regions or g:N blocks as evidence, never only p:N.
dimensions.structure: Article order, heading levels, list type/depth/order, footnotes. DOM id is not quality. Cite s:N headings/list items or g:N blocks as evidence, never only p:N.
dimensions.title: Faithful article title including chapter numbers; omit permalink controls.
dimensions.format: Code whitespace and meaningful block formatting. No code/format requirement: not_applicable.

anchors.4: No material defect observed in supplied scope
anchors.3: Small local defect (e.g. missing title number)

completeness.reason: short explanation

evidence.quote: verbatim nonempty substring (whitespace runs folded for matching), max 400 chars

cleanliness.reason: short explanation

evidence.quote: verbatim nonempty substring (whitespace runs folded for matching), max 400 chars

structure.reason: short explanation

evidence.quote: verbatim nonempty substring (whitespace runs folded for matching), max 400 chars

title.reason: short explanation

evidence.quote: verbatim nonempty substring (whitespace runs folded for matching), max 400 chars

format.reason: short explanation

evidence.quote: verbatim nonempty substring (whitespace runs folded for matching), max 400 chars

constraints: Exactly schema_version and dimensions at top level; exactly the five dimensions and their five keys.
Scored/partial require integer score and 1..8 citations. Null for unscored/not_applicable.

SCORING INDEPENDENCE: Determine each score and severity SOLELY from the actual defect magnitude observed by comparing the candidate against source/gold, strictly per the anchors (4=no material defect, 3=small local defect, 2=clear moderate loss or contamination, 1=large defect, 0=empty or fundamentally incorrect). Severity follows the defect itself: none=no material defect, minor=small local defect, major=clear moderate loss/contamination or wrong order/attributes, critical=empty/fundamentally wrong or severe order loss. evidence_menus is a CITATION APPENDIX placed after the data for convenience ONLY; the presence, absence, wording or quantity of suggested evidence MUST NOT raise or lower any score or severity. Never infer defect severity from which evidence is suggested.
not_applicable is allowed only for format and requires severity none, score null, evidence []. unscored requires severity unknown, score null, evidence [].

EVERY scored/partial dimension MUST cite at least one s: or g: reference. Candidate-only p: evidence is rejected for every dimension, including cleanliness and structure. Scores below 4 need concrete defect evidence.

For cleanliness cite the source regions that must be excluded (s:N navigation/ads/footer) or g:N blocks proving noise absence; for structure cite s:N or g:N blocks showing expected order, levels and list attributes.

Quotes must be short (<=120 chars) verbatim substrings of the cited evidence. Whitespace runs (including U+00A0 non-breaking spaces, tabs, newlines and repeated spaces) are folded to single spaces for matching; every non-whitespace character must still appear verbatim and in order. Never paraphrase or reorder words. evidence_menus is a citation appendix listed after the data; it provides ready-to-cite {ref, quote} pairs copied exactly from the supplied evidence. You may use them directly or cite any other listed ref with your own verbatim quote. The appendix is for citation convenience only and must not influence scoring; the s:/g: citation rule still applies. Empty candidate has no p-block to cite; source evidence suffices.

p:N and g:N are zero-based indices into the supplied candidate.blocks and gold.blocks arrays; block_count gives the array length. Cite only refs present in the supplied lists; never cite an index at or beyond block_count or invent refs.
When source.truncated is true, prefer s:N node citations over s:html and mark every scored dimension partial.
Use partial if source HTML is truncated. Source-only scores are provisional, not gold-validated.
Do not invent confidence values. Unknown or missing evidence requires unscored with reason.
Missing title number is title=3/minor. Empty output with nonempty article: completeness=0/critical.
Format scope excludes link correctness and rendered CSS. Output brief reasons, not hidden reasoning.

NPR > Debating Data Centers

How the movement against data centers has gone global

By Ruth Sherlock

Monday, November 16, 2026 • 4:44 AM EST

Heard on Morning Edition

At a demonstration in downtown Zaragoza in Spain, grandmothers, moms with babies in carriers, teenagers filled an entire avenue as they called to stop a Microsoft data center from being built beside a beloved local forest.

Videos of the loud opposition to data centers in the United States helped inspire university student Monica Gracia to show up.

"I think that's one of the reasons why this place is so full of people," said Gracia.

While many environmental problems are often very local, most of the push to build data centers around the world comes from U.S. tech giants. So opponents fighting new data centers are teaming up across continents.

"We have connections with of course the USA, Africa, Australia and even some parts of Asia," said Aurora Gomez, a Spanish activist. "We are coordinated and we are together."

Gomez founded the group Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio, which translates to 'Your Cloud Dries My River,' to stop a data centre in her home town, Talavera La Reina in Spain.

"It was meant to be a weeklong campaign to raise local awareness," she told NPR. "But it just caught fire, because there are so many data centers coming to Spain and to every part of the world."

Gomez said she now fields dozens of emails a day from residents of communities where data centers are planned.

She was recently part of a wider European effort that coordinated a series of protests against data centers in 15 countries over two days under the banner "Stop Dirty Data Centres," demanding an immediate moratorium on large-scale projects.

"We are gaining so much traction - our narratives are being spread around the world," Gomez said.

More than 70 European projects were rejected or restricted in the first four months of 2026 alone, according to the European Data Centre Monitor. Public opposition has delayed or cancelled some $42 billion of data center spending in Europe, according to a report from consulting firm STL Partners.

Shared tactics, crowdfunding

The groups share tactics. After activists in the UK used crowdfunding to launch a successful legal effort to stop a large data center northwest of London, Gomez said she and other Spanish activists were inspired to do the same.

It took them only a week to raise the money they needed to mount what they say is the first major legal challenge in Spain against data center expansion, in this instance to be prevent the Aragón regional government from allowing Amazon Web Service to build one of its largest data center hubs outside the U.S.

"We are exercising our rights," said Luis Garcia from Ecologistas in Acción, one of the groups involved in the case.  "We know they have way more means than we do. But the crowdfunding proves we have gathered a lot of support from so many people, individuals, organizations."

The movement is both global and hyperlocal.

In the tiny village of Cuarte on the rural plains of Aragon, colorful bunting flaps in the wind in the main square beside a Baroque church from a recent celebration by the town's tight-knit community. Strung up on a wall is a giant banner that reads, "We drink water, not data centers."

It's a slogan to protest a giant Amazon facility that's under construction at the edge of the village.

The drilling and hammering of construction interrupts the dawn chorus of the birds. Clouds of dust fill the air and the ground trembles as trucks race piles of freshly dug earth to the site which sits between the village and a protected wetland.

"To us this feels like a seven-headed monster," said Carlos Olivan, a resident of Cuarte. "We're trying, in a very small group, to make visible the scale of what is happening, so people understand, empathise, and mobilize."

The residents began with a local survey they call a "referendum" in the village, with 144 registered voters – close to the entire voting age population – responding via WhatsApp. 95% of respondents were against these centers. "And we think the other five made a mistake filling out the forms," said Olivan.

The villagers shared the results with local media and took them to town hall meetings and to officials in the regional government. And they want to pressure the authorities to hold a wider referendum to give residents across the entire province a voice in decisions about these data center developments that promise to transform the region.

In all, planning documents show the regional government is processing approvals for 27 data center complexes, one is close to the size of New York City's Central Park. Together it's estimated they'll require many more times the electricity the region currently uses, and consume vast quantities of water in an area already blighted by drought.

David Blasquez, the head of public policy for Amazon Web Services in Spain and Portugal, told NPR the company is doing all it can to be a "best in class" neighbor, including fixing local water pipes to conserve the resource. The regional government told NPR how much water a data center consumes is considered when they weigh planning permission.

But Laura Coscuella, a resident of a town close to where several facilities are planned, said she joined a local group No Es Sequia Es Saqeo – "It's Not Drought, It's Plunder," to fight these developments after learning of the environmental problems some U.S. communities have faced. "We have a lot of data from the U.S. especially. We need everyone to know about this. I'm afraid that people won't notice what is happening until it's too late – until the taps are not working because they have run the water dry."

Coscuella is helping residents of Cuarte become even more effective in their opposition by using strategies in part learned from this wider coordinated network. Each resident plays to their strength, be it searching complex planning documents or planning direct actions.

At the protest in downtown Zaragoza in Aragon, local activist María Peña Calvo said when dealing with companies sensitive to public opinion, every act of opposition matters even if it feels small. "Putting stones in their path can make some companies simply give up or go elsewhere."

"It was meant to be a weeklong campaign to raise local awareness," she told NPR. "But it just caught fire, because there are so many data centers coming to Spain and to every part of the world."

She was recently part of a wider European effort that coordinated a series of protests against data centers in 15 countries over two days under the banner "Stop Dirty Data Centres," demanding an immediate moratorium on large-scale projects.

NPR > Debating Data Centers

How the movement against data centers has gone global

By Ruth Sherlock

Monday, November 16, 2026 • 4:44 AM EST

Heard on Morning Edition

At a demonstration in downtown Zaragoza in Spain, grandmothers, moms with babies in carriers, teenagers filled an entire avenue as they called to stop a Microsoft data center from being built beside a beloved local forest.

Videos of the loud opposition to data centers in the United States helped inspire university student Monica Gracia to show up.

"I think that's one of the reasons why this place is so full of people," said Gracia.

While many environmental problems are often very local, most of the push to build data centers around the world comes from U.S. tech giants. So opponents fighting new data centers are teaming up across continents.

"We have connections with of course the USA, Africa, Australia and even some parts of Asia," said Aurora Gomez, a Spanish activist. "We are coordinated and we are together."

Gomez founded the group Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio, which translates to 'Your Cloud Dries My River,' to stop a data centre in her home town, Talavera La Reina in Spain.

"It was meant to be a weeklong campaign to raise local awareness," she told NPR. "But it just caught fire, because there are so many data centers coming to Spain and to every part of the world."

Gomez said she now fields dozens of emails a day from residents of communities where data centers are planned.

She was recently part of a wider European effort that coordinated a series of protests against data centers in 15 countries over two days under the banner "Stop Dirty Data Centres," demanding an immediate moratorium on large-scale projects.

"We are gaining so much traction - our narratives are being spread around the world," Gomez said.

More than 70 European projects were rejected or restricted in the first four months of 2026 alone, according to the European Data Centre Monitor. Public opposition has delayed or cancelled some $42 billion of data center spending in Europe, according to a report from consulting firm STL Partners.

Shared tactics, crowdfunding

The groups share tactics. After activists in the UK used crowdfunding to launch a successful legal effort to stop a large data center northwest of London, Gomez said she and other Spanish activists were inspired to do the same.

It took them only a week to raise the money they needed to mount what they say is the first major legal challenge in Spain against data center expansion, in this instance to be prevent the Aragón regional government from allowing Amazon Web Service to build one of its largest data center hubs outside the U.S.

"We are exercising our rights," said Luis Garcia from Ecologistas in Acción, one of the groups involved in the case.  "We know they have way more means than we do. But the crowdfunding proves we have gathered a lot of support from so many people, individuals, organizations."

The movement is both global and hyperlocal.

In the tiny village of Cuarte on the rural plains of Aragon, colorful bunting flaps in the wind in the main square beside a Baroque church from a recent celebration by the town's tight-knit community. Strung up on a wall is a giant banner that reads, "We drink water, not data centers."

It's a slogan to protest a giant Amazon facility that's under construction at the edge of the village.

The drilling and hammering of construction interrupts the dawn chorus of the birds. Clouds of dust fill the air and the ground trembles as trucks race piles of freshly dug earth to the site which sits between the village and a protected wetland.

"To us this feels like a seven-headed monster," said Carlos Olivan, a resident of Cuarte. "We're trying, in a very small group, to make visible the scale of what is happening, so people understand, empathise, and mobilize."

The residents began with a local survey they call a "referendum" in the village, with 144 registered voters – close to the entire voting age population – responding via WhatsApp. 95% of respondents were against these centers. "And we think the other five made a mistake filling out the forms," said Olivan.

The villagers shared the results with local media and took them to town hall meetings and to officials in the regional government. And they want to pressure the authorities to hold a wider referendum to give residents across the entire province a voice in decisions about these data center developments that promise to transform the region.

In all, planning documents show the regional government is processing approvals for 27 data center complexes, one is close to the size of New York City's Central Park. Together it's estimated they'll require many more times the electricity the region currently uses, and consume vast quantities of water in an area already blighted by drought.

David Blasquez, the head of public policy for Amazon Web Services in Spain and Portugal, told NPR the company is doing all it can to be a "best in class" neighbor, including fixing local water pipes to conserve the resource. The regional government told NPR how much water a data center consumes is considered when they weigh planning permission.

But Laura Coscuella, a resident of a town close to where several facilities are planned, said she joined a local group No Es Sequia Es Saqeo – "It's Not Drought, It's Plunder," to fight these developments after learning of the environmental problems some U.S. communities have faced. "We have a lot of data from the U.S. especially. We need everyone to know about this. I'm afraid that people won't notice what is happening until it's too late – until the taps are not working because they have run the water dry."

Coscuella is helping residents of Cuarte become even more effective in their opposition by using strategies in part learned from this wider coordinated network. Each resident plays to their strength, be it searching complex planning documents or planning direct actions.

At the protest in downtown Zaragoza in Aragon, local activist María Peña Calvo said when dealing with companies sensitive to public opinion, every act of opposition matters even if it feels small. "Putting stones in their path can make some companies simply give up or go elsewhere."

          Debating Data Centers
How the movement against data centers has gone global
By Ruth Sherlock
Monday, November 16, 2026 • 4:44 AM EST
Heard on Morning Edition

At a demonstration in downtown Zaragoza in Spain, grandmothers, moms with babies in carriers, teenagers filled an entire avenue as they called to stop a Microsoft data center from being built beside a beloved local forest.
Videos of the loud opposition to data centers in the United States helped inspire university student Monica Gracia to show up.
"I think that's one of the reasons why this place is so full of people," said Gracia.

While many environmental problems are often very local, most of the push to build data centers around the world comes from U.S. tech giants. So opponents fighting new data centers are teaming up across continents.
"We have connections with of course the USA, Africa, Australia and even some parts of Asia," said Aurora Gomez, a Spanish activist. "We are coordinated and we are together."
Gomez founded the group Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio, which translates to 'Your Cloud Dries My River,' to stop a data centre in her home town, Talavera La Reina in Spain.
"It was meant to be a weeklong campaign to raise local awareness," she told NPR. "But it just caught fire, because there are so many data centers coming to Spain and to every part of the world."
Gomez said she now fields dozens of emails a day from residents of communities where data centers are planned.

She was recently part of a wider European effort that coordinated a series of protests against data centers in 15 countries over two days under the banner "Stop Dirty Data Centres," demanding an immediate moratorium on large-scale projects.
"We are gaining so much traction - our narratives are being spread around the world," Gomez said.

More than 70 European projects were rejected or restricted in the first four months of 2026 alone, according to the European Data Centre Monitor. Public opposition has delayed or cancelled some $42 billion of data center spending in Europe, according to a report from consulting firm STL Partners.
Shared tactics, crowdfunding

The groups share tactics. After activists in the UK used crowdfunding to launch a successful legal effort to stop a large data center northwest of London, Gomez said she and other Spanish activists were inspired to do the same.

It took them only a week to raise the money they needed to mount what they say is the first major legal challenge in Spain against data center expansion, in this instance to be prevent the Aragón regional government from allowing Amazon Web Service to build one of its largest data center hubs outside the U.S.

"We are exercising our rights," said Luis Garcia from Ecologistas in Acción, one of the groups involved in the case.  "We know they have way more means than we do. But the crowdfunding proves we have gathered a lot of support from so many people, individuals, organizations."
The movement is both global and hyperlocal.

In the tiny village of Cuarte on the rural plains of Aragon, colorful bunting flaps in the wind in the main square beside a Baroque church from a recent celebration by the town's tight-knit community. Strung up on a wall is a giant banner that reads, "We drink water, not data centers."
It's a slogan to protest a giant Amazon facility that's under construction at the edge of the village.

The drilling and hammering of construction interrupts the dawn chorus of the birds. Clouds of dust fill the air and the ground trembles as trucks race piles of freshly dug earth to the site which sits between the village and a protected wetland.

"To us this feels like a seven-headed monster," said Carlos Olivan, a resident of Cuarte. "We're trying, in a very small group, to make visible the scale of what is happening, so people understand, empathise, and mobilize."

The residents began with a local survey they call a "referendum" in the village, with 144 registered voters – close to the entire voting age population – responding via WhatsApp. 95% of respondents were against these centers. "And we think the other five made a mistake filling out the forms," said Olivan.

The villagers shared the results with local media and took them to town hall meetings and to officials in the regional government. And they want to pressure the authorities to hold a wider referendum to give residents across the entire province a voice in decisions about these data center developments that promise to transform the region.

In all, planning documents show the regional government is processing approvals for 27 data center complexes, one is close to the size of New York City's Central Park. Together it's estimated they'll require many more times the electricity the region currently uses, and consume vast quantities of water in an area already blighted by drought.

David Blasquez, the head of public policy for Amazon Web Services in Spain and Portugal, told NPR the company is doing all it can to be a "best in class" neighbor, including fixing local water pipes to conserve the resource. The regional government told NPR how much water a data center consumes is considered when they weigh planning permission.

But Laura Coscuella, a resident of a town close to where several facilities are planned, said she joined a local group No Es Sequia Es Saqeo – "It's Not Drought, It's Plunder," to fight these developments after learning of the environmental problems some U.S. communities have faced. "We have a lot of data from the U.S. especially. We need everyone to know about this. I'm afraid that people won't notice what is happening until it's too late – until the taps are not working because they have run the water dry."

Coscuella is helping residents of Cuarte become even more effective in their opposition by using strategies in part learned from this wider coordinated network. Each resident plays to their strength, be it searching complex planning documents or planning direct actions.

At the protest in downtown Zaragoza in Aragon, local activist María Peña Calvo said when dealing with companies sensitive to public opinion, every act of opposition matters even if it feels small. "Putting stones in their path can make some companies simply give up or go elsewhere."

NPR > Debating Data Centers

How the movement against data centers has gone global

By Ruth Sherlock

Monday, November 16, 2026 • 4:44 AM EST

Heard on Morning Edition

At a demonstration in downtown Zaragoza in Spain, grandmothers, moms with babies in carriers, teenagers filled an entire avenue as they called to stop a Microsoft data center from being built beside a beloved local forest.

Videos of the loud opposition to data centers in the United States helped inspire university student Monica Gracia to show up.

"I think that's one of the reasons why this place is so full of people," said Gracia.

While many environmental problems are often very local, most of the push to build data centers around the world comes from U.S. tech giants. So opponents fighting new data centers are teaming up across continents.

"We have connections with of course the USA, Africa, Australia and even some parts of Asia," said Aurora Gomez, a Spanish activist. "We are coordinated and we are together."

Gomez founded the group Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio, which translates to 'Your Cloud Dries My River,' to stop a data centre in her home town, Talavera La Reina in Spain.

"It was meant to be a weeklong campaign to raise local awareness," she told NPR. "But it just caught fire, because there are so many data centers coming to Spain and to every part of the world."

Gomez said she now fields dozens of emails a day from residents of communities where data centers are planned.

She was recently part of a wider European effort that coordinated a series of protests against data centers in 15 countries over two days under the banner "Stop Dirty Data Centres," demanding an immediate moratorium on large-scale projects.

"We are gaining so much traction - our narratives are being spread around the world," Gomez said.

More than 70 European projects were rejected or restricted in the first four months of 2026 alone, according to the European Data Centre Monitor. Public opposition has delayed or cancelled some $42 billion of data center spending in Europe, according to a report from consulting firm STL Partners.

Shared tactics, crowdfunding

The groups share tactics. After activists in the UK used crowdfunding to launch a successful legal effort to stop a large data center northwest of London, Gomez said she and other Spanish activists were inspired to do the same.

It took them only a week to raise the money they needed to mount what they say is the first major legal challenge in Spain against data center expansion, in this instance to be prevent the Aragón regional government from allowing Amazon Web Service to build one of its largest data center hubs outside the U.S.

"We are exercising our rights," said Luis Garcia from Ecologistas in Acción, one of the groups involved in the case.  "We know they have way more means than we do. But the crowdfunding proves we have gathered a lot of support from so many people, individuals, organizations."

The movement is both global and hyperlocal.

In the tiny village of Cuarte on the rural plains of Aragon, colorful bunting flaps in the wind in the main square beside a Baroque church from a recent celebration by the town's tight-knit community. Strung up on a wall is a giant banner that reads, "We drink water, not data centers."

It's a slogan to protest a giant Amazon facility that's under construction at the edge of the village.

The drilling and hammering of construction interrupts the dawn chorus of the birds. Clouds of dust fill the air and the ground trembles as trucks race piles of freshly dug earth to the site which sits between the village and a protected wetland.

"To us this feels like a seven-headed monster," said Carlos Olivan, a resident of Cuarte. "We're trying, in a very small group, to make visible the scale of what is happening, so people understand, empathise, and mobilize."

The residents began with a local survey they call a "referendum" in the village, with 144 registered voters – close to the entire voting age population – responding via WhatsApp. 95% of respondents were against these centers. "And we think the other five made a mistake filling out the forms," said Olivan.

The villagers shared the results with local media and took them to town hall meetings and to officials in the regional government. And they want to pressure the authorities to hold a wider referendum to give residents across the entire province a voice in decisions about these data center developments that promise to transform the region.

In all, planning documents show the regional government is processing approvals for 27 data center complexes, one is close to the size of New York City's Central Park. Together it's estimated they'll require many more times the electricity the region currently uses, and consume vast quantities of water in an area already blighted by drought.

David Blasquez, the head of public policy for Amazon Web Services in Spain and Portugal, told NPR the company is doing all it can to be a "best in class" neighbor, including fixing local water pipes to conserve the resource. The regional government told NPR how much water a data center consumes is considered when they weigh planning permission.

But Laura Coscuella, a resident of a town close to where several facilities are planned, said she joined a local group No Es Sequia Es Saqeo – "It's Not Drought, It's Plunder," to fight these developments after learning of the environmental problems some U.S. communities have faced. "We have a lot of data from the U.S. especially. We need everyone to know about this. I'm afraid that people won't notice what is happening until it's too late – until the taps are not working because they have run the water dry."

Coscuella is helping residents of Cuarte become even more effective in their opposition by using strategies in part learned from this wider coordinated network. Each resident plays to their strength, be it searching complex planning documents or planning direct actions.

At the protest in downtown Zaragoza in Aragon, local activist María Peña Calvo said when dealing with companies sensitive to public opinion, every act of opposition matters even if it feels small. "Putting stones in their path can make some companies simply give up or go elsewhere."

The opposition to data centers that American voters expressed in the midterms is a worldwide phenomenon. Voters around the U.S. have made it harder for communities to build big projects tied to artificial intelligence. And in other countries, local groups are joining forces to slow the AI buildout. NPR's Ruth Sherlock reports.

          Debating Data Centers
How the movement against data centers has gone global
By Ruth Sherlock
Monday, November 16, 2026 • 4:44 AM EST
Heard on Morning Edition

At a demonstration in downtown Zaragoza in Spain, grandmothers, moms with babies in carriers, teenagers filled an entire avenue as they called to stop a Microsoft data center from being built beside a beloved local forest.
Videos of the loud opposition to data centers in the United States helped inspire university student Monica Gracia to show up.
"I think that's one of the reasons why this place is so full of people," said Gracia.

While many environmental problems are often very local, most of the push to build data centers around the world comes from U.S. tech giants. So opponents fighting new data centers are teaming up across continents.
"We have connections with of course the USA, Africa, Australia and even some parts of Asia," said Aurora Gomez, a Spanish activist. "We are coordinated and we are together."
Gomez founded the group Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio, which translates to 'Your Cloud Dries My River,' to stop a data centre in her home town, Talavera La Reina in Spain.
"It was meant to be a weeklong campaign to raise local awareness," she told NPR. "But it just caught fire, because there are so many data centers coming to Spain and to every part of the world."
Gomez said she now fields dozens of emails a day from residents of communities where data centers are planned.

She was recently part of a wider European effort that coordinated a series of protests against data centers in 15 countries over two days under the banner "Stop Dirty Data Centres," demanding an immediate moratorium on large-scale projects.
"We are gaining so much traction - our narratives are being spread around the world," Gomez said.

More than 70 European projects were rejected or restricted in the first four months of 2026 alone, according to the European Data Centre Monitor. Public opposition has delayed or cancelled some $42 billion of data center spending in Europe, according to a report from consulting firm STL Partners.
Shared tactics, crowdfunding

The groups share tactics. After activists in the UK used crowdfunding to launch a successful legal effort to stop a large data center northwest of London, Gomez said she and other Spanish activists were inspired to do the same.

It took them only a week to raise the money they needed to mount what they say is the first major legal challenge in Spain against data center expansion, in this instance to be prevent the Aragón regional government from allowing Amazon Web Service to build one of its largest data center hubs outside the U.S.

"We are exercising our rights," said Luis Garcia from Ecologistas in Acción, one of the groups involved in the case.  "We know they have way more means than we do. But the crowdfunding proves we have gathered a lot of support from so many people, individuals, organizations."
The movement is both global and hyperlocal.

In the tiny village of Cuarte on the rural plains of Aragon, colorful bunting flaps in the wind in the main square beside a Baroque church from a recent celebration by the town's tight-knit community. Strung up on a wall is a giant banner that reads, "We drink water, not data centers."
It's a slogan to protest a giant Amazon facility that's under construction at the edge of the village.

The drilling and hammering of construction interrupts the dawn chorus of the birds. Clouds of dust fill the air and the ground trembles as trucks race piles of freshly dug earth to the site which sits between the village and a protected wetland.

"To us this feels like a seven-headed monster," said Carlos Olivan, a resident of Cuarte. "We're trying, in a very small group, to make visible the scale of what is happening, so people understand, empathise, and mobilize."

The residents began with a local survey they call a "referendum" in the village, with 144 registered voters – close to the entire voting age population – responding via WhatsApp. 95% of respondents were against these centers. "And we think the other five made a mistake filling out the forms," said Olivan.

The villagers shared the results with local media and took them to town hall meetings and to officials in the regional government. And they want to pressure the authorities to hold a wider referendum to give residents across the entire province a voice in decisions about these data center developments that promise to transform the region.

In all, planning documents show the regional government is processing approvals for 27 data center complexes, one is close to the size of New York City's Central Park. Together it's estimated they'll require many more times the electricity the region currently uses, and consume vast quantities of water in an area already blighted by drought.

David Blasquez, the head of public policy for Amazon Web Services in Spain and Portugal, told NPR the company is doing all it can to be a "best in class" neighbor, including fixing local water pipes to conserve the resource. The regional government told NPR how much water a data center consumes is considered when they weigh planning permission.

But Laura Coscuella, a resident of a town close to where several facilities are planned, said she joined a local group No Es Sequia Es Saqeo – "It's Not Drought, It's Plunder," to fight these developments after learning of the environmental problems some U.S. communities have faced. "We have a lot of data from the U.S. especially. We need everyone to know about this. I'm afraid that people won't notice what is happening until it's too late – until the taps are not working because they have run the water dry."

Coscuella is helping residents of Cuarte become even more effective in their opposition by using strategies in part learned from this wider coordinated network. Each resident plays to their strength, be it searching complex planning documents or planning direct actions.

At the protest in downtown Zaragoza in Aragon, local activist María Peña Calvo said when dealing with companies sensitive to public opinion, every act of opposition matters even if it feels small. "Putting stones in their path can make some companies simply give up or go elsewhere."

Your Freedom Needs Free Software

by Richard Stallman

Many of us know that governments can threaten the human rights of software users through censorship and surveillance of the Internet. Many do not realize that the software they run on their home or work computers can be an even worse threat. Thinking of software as “just a tool,” they suppose that it obeys them, when in fact it often obeys others instead.

The software running in most computers is nonfree, proprietary software: controlled by software companies, not by its users. Users can't check what these programs do, nor prevent them from doing what they don't want. Most people accept this because they have seen no other way, but it is simply wrong to give developers power over the users' computer.

This unjust power, as usual, tempts its wielders to further misdeeds. If a computer talks to a network, and you don't control the software in it, it can easily spy on you. Microsoft Windows spies on users; for instance, it reports what words a user searches for in her own files, and what other programs are installed. RealPlayer spies too; it reports what the user plays. Cell phones are full of nonfree software, which spies. Cell phones send out localizing signals even when “off,” many can send out your precise GPS location whether you wish or not, and some models can be switched on remotely as listening devices. Users can't fix these malicious features because they don't have control.

Some proprietary software is designed to restrict and attack its users. Windows Vista was a big advance in this field; the reason it required replacement of old hardware is that the new models were designed to support unbreakable restrictions. Microsoft thus required users to pay for shiny new shackles. Vista was also designed to permit forced updating by corporate authority. Hence the Bad Vista campaign, which urged Windows users not to “upgrade” to Vista. For later Windows versions, which are even more malicious, we now have Upgrade from Windows. Mac OS also contains features designed to restrict its users.

In 1999, Microsoft installed back doors for the US government's use. Researchers disagree on what those back doors can do, but Microsoft has made that question less important by its forced software installation, which is even worse. If the 1999 code won't let NSA spy on you, Microsoft can force another change which will do so. Other proprietary programs may or may not have back doors, but since we cannot check them, we cannot trust them.

The only way to assure that your software is working for you is to insist on free/libre software. This means users get the source code, are free to study and change it, and are free to redistribute it with or without changes. The GNU/Linux system, developed specifically for users' freedom, includes office applications, multimedia, games, and everything you really need to run a computer. See our list of totally free/libre versions of GNU/Linux.

A special problem occurs when activists for social change use proprietary software, because its developers, who control it, may be companies they wish to protest—or that work hand in glove with the states whose policies they oppose. Control of our software by a proprietary software company, whether it be Microsoft, Apple, Adobe or Skype, means control of what we can say, and to whom. This threatens our freedom in all areas of life.

There is also danger in using a company's server to do your word processing or email—and not just if you are in China, as US lawyer Michael Springmann discovered. In 2003, AOL not only handed over to the police his confidential discussions with clients, it also made his email and his address list disappear, and didn't admit this was intentional until one of its staff made a slip. Springmann gave up on getting his data back.

The US is not the only state that doesn't respect human rights, so keep your data on your own computer, and your backups under your own custody—and run your computer with free/libre software.

Your Freedom Needs Free Software

by Richard Stallman

Many of us know that governments can threaten the human rights of software users through censorship and surveillance of the Internet. Many do not realize that the software they run on their home or work computers can be an even worse threat. Thinking of software as “just a tool,” they suppose that it obeys them, when in fact it often obeys others instead.

The software running in most computers is nonfree, proprietary software: controlled by software companies, not by its users. Users can't check what these programs do, nor prevent them from doing what they don't want. Most people accept this because they have seen no other way, but it is simply wrong to give developers power over the users' computer.

This unjust power, as usual, tempts its wielders to further misdeeds. If a computer talks to a network, and you don't control the software in it, it can easily spy on you. Microsoft Windows spies on users; for instance, it reports what words a user searches for in her own files, and what other programs are installed. RealPlayer spies too; it reports what the user plays. Cell phones are full of nonfree software, which spies. Cell phones send out localizing signals even when “off,” many can send out your precise GPS location whether you wish or not, and some models can be switched on remotely as listening devices. Users can't fix these malicious features because they don't have control.

Some proprietary software is designed to restrict and attack its users. Windows Vista was a big advance in this field; the reason it required replacement of old hardware is that the new models were designed to support unbreakable restrictions. Microsoft thus required users to pay for shiny new shackles. Vista was also designed to permit forced updating by corporate authority. Hence the Bad Vista campaign, which urged Windows users not to “upgrade” to Vista. For later Windows versions, which are even more malicious, we now have Upgrade from Windows. Mac OS also contains features designed to restrict its users.

In 1999, Microsoft installed back doors for the US government's use. Researchers disagree on what those back doors can do, but Microsoft has made that question less important by its forced software installation, which is even worse. If the 1999 code won't let NSA spy on you, Microsoft can force another change which will do so. Other proprietary programs may or may not have back doors, but since we cannot check them, we cannot trust them.

The only way to assure that your software is working for you is to insist on free/libre software. This means users get the source code, are free to study and change it, and are free to redistribute it with or without changes. The GNU/Linux system, developed specifically for users' freedom, includes office applications, multimedia, games, and everything you really need to run a computer. See our list of totally free/libre versions of GNU/Linux.

A special problem occurs when activists for social change use proprietary software, because its developers, who control it, may be companies they wish to protest—or that work hand in glove with the states whose policies they oppose. Control of our software by a proprietary software company, whether it be Microsoft, Apple, Adobe or Skype, means control of what we can say, and to whom. This threatens our freedom in all areas of life.

There is also danger in using a company's server to do your word processing or email—and not just if you are in China, as US lawyer Michael Springmann discovered. In 2003, AOL not only handed over to the police his confidential discussions with clients, it also made his email and his address list disappear, and didn't admit this was intentional until one of its staff made a slip. Springmann gave up on getting his data back.

The US is not the only state that doesn't respect human rights, so keep your data on your own computer, and your backups under your own custody—and run your computer with free/libre software.

Your Freedom Needs Free Software

by Richard Stallman

Many of us know that governments can threaten the human rights of software users through censorship and surveillance of the Internet. Many do not realize that the software they run on their home or work computers can be an even worse threat. Thinking of software as “just a tool,” they suppose that it obeys them, when in fact it often obeys others instead.

The software running in most computers is nonfree, proprietary software: controlled by software companies, not by its users. Users can't check what these programs do, nor prevent them from doing what they don't want. Most people accept this because they have seen no other way, but it is simply wrong to give developers power over the users' computer.

This unjust power, as usual, tempts its wielders to further misdeeds. If a computer talks to a network, and you don't control the software in it, it can easily spy on you. Microsoft Windows spies on users; for instance, it reports what words a user searches for in her own files, and what other programs are installed. RealPlayer spies too; it reports what the user plays. Cell phones are full of nonfree software, which spies. Cell phones send out localizing signals even when “off,” many can send out your precise GPS location whether you wish or not, and some models can be switched on remotely as listening devices. Users can't fix these malicious features because they don't have control.

Some proprietary software is designed to restrict and attack its users. Windows Vista was a big advance in this field; the reason it required replacement of old hardware is that the new models were designed to support unbreakable restrictions. Microsoft thus required users to pay for shiny new shackles. Vista was also designed to permit forced updating by corporate authority. Hence the Bad Vista campaign, which urged Windows users not to “upgrade” to Vista. For later Windows versions, which are even more malicious, we now have Upgrade from Windows. Mac OS also contains features designed to restrict its users.

In 1999, Microsoft installed back doors for the US government's use. Researchers disagree on what those back doors can do, but Microsoft has made that question less important by its forced software installation, which is even worse. If the 1999 code won't let NSA spy on you, Microsoft can force another change which will do so. Other proprietary programs may or may not have back doors, but since we cannot check them, we cannot trust them.

The only way to assure that your software is working for you is to insist on free/libre software. This means users get the source code, are free to study and change it, and are free to redistribute it with or without changes. The GNU/Linux system, developed specifically for users' freedom, includes office applications, multimedia, games, and everything you really need to run a computer. See our list of totally free/libre versions of GNU/Linux.

A special problem occurs when activists for social change use proprietary software, because its developers, who control it, may be companies they wish to protest—or that work hand in glove with the states whose policies they oppose. Control of our software by a proprietary software company, whether it be Microsoft, Apple, Adobe or Skype, means control of what we can say, and to whom. This threatens our freedom in all areas of life.

There is also danger in using a company's server to do your word processing or email—and not just if you are in China, as US lawyer Michael Springmann discovered. In 2003, AOL not only handed over to the police his confidential discussions with clients, it also made his email and his address list disappear, and didn't admit this was intentional until one of its staff made a slip. Springmann gave up on getting his data back.

The US is not the only state that doesn't respect human rights, so keep your data on your own computer, and your backups under your own custody—and run your computer with free/libre software.

Your Freedom Needs Free Software

by Richard Stallman

Many of us know that governments can threaten the human rights of software users through censorship and surveillance of the Internet. Many do not realize that the software they run on their home or work computers can be an even worse threat. Thinking of software as “just a tool,” they suppose that it obeys them, when in fact it often obeys others instead.

The software running in most computers is nonfree, proprietary software: controlled by software companies, not by its users. Users can't check what these programs do, nor prevent them from doing what they don't want. Most people accept this because they have seen no other way, but it is simply wrong to give developers power over the users' computer.

This unjust power, as usual, tempts its wielders to further misdeeds. If a computer talks to a network, and you don't control the software in it, it can easily spy on you. Microsoft Windows spies on users; for instance, it reports what words a user searches for in her own files, and what other programs are installed. RealPlayer spies too; it reports what the user plays. Cell phones are full of nonfree software, which spies. Cell phones send out localizing signals even when “off,” many can send out your precise GPS location whether you wish or not, and some models can be switched on remotely as listening devices. Users can't fix these malicious features because they don't have control.

Some proprietary software is designed to restrict and attack its users. Windows Vista was a big advance in this field; the reason it required replacement of old hardware is that the new models were designed to support unbreakable restrictions. Microsoft thus required users to pay for shiny new shackles. Vista was also designed to permit forced updating by corporate authority. Hence the Bad Vista campaign, which urged Windows users not to “upgrade” to Vista. For later Windows versions, which are even more malicious, we now have Upgrade from Windows. Mac OS also contains features designed to restrict its users.

In 1999, Microsoft installed back doors for the US government's use. Researchers disagree on what those back doors can do, but Microsoft has made that question less important by its forced software installation, which is even worse. If the 1999 code won't let NSA spy on you, Microsoft can force another change which will do so. Other proprietary programs may or may not have back doors, but since we cannot check them, we cannot trust them.

The only way to assure that your software is working for you is to insist on free/libre software. This means users get the source code, are free to study and change it, and are free to redistribute it with or without changes. The GNU/Linux system, developed specifically for users' freedom, includes office applications, multimedia, games, and everything you really need to run a computer. See our list of totally free/libre versions of GNU/Linux.

A special problem occurs when activists for social change use proprietary software, because its developers, who control it, may be companies they wish to protest—or that work hand in glove with the states whose policies they oppose. Control of our software by a proprietary software company, whether it be Microsoft, Apple, Adobe or Skype, means control of what we can say, and to whom. This threatens our freedom in all areas of life.

There is also danger in using a company's server to do your word processing or email—and not just if you are in China, as US lawyer Michael Springmann discovered. In 2003, AOL not only handed over to the police his confidential discussions with clients, it also made his email and his address list disappear, and didn't admit this was intentional until one of its staff made a slip. Springmann gave up on getting his data back.

The US is not the only state that doesn't respect human rights, so keep your data on your own computer, and your backups under your own custody—and run your computer with free/libre software.

Your Freedom Needs Free Software

Many of us know that governments can threaten the human rights of
software users through censorship and surveillance of the Internet.
Many do not realize that the software they run on their home or work
computers can be an even worse threat.  Thinking of software as
“just a tool,” they suppose that it obeys them, when in
fact it often obeys others instead.

The software running in most computers is nonfree,
proprietary software: controlled by software companies, not
by its users.  Users can't check what these programs do, nor
prevent them from doing what they don't want.  Most people accept
this because they have seen no other way, but it is simply wrong
to give developers power over the users' computer.

This unjust power, as usual, tempts its wielders to further
misdeeds. If a computer talks to a network, and you don't control the
software in it, it can easily spy on you.  Microsoft Windows spies on
users; for instance, it reports what words a user searches for in her
own files, and what other programs are installed.  RealPlayer spies
too; it reports what the user plays.  Cell phones are full of nonfree
software, which spies.  Cell phones send out localizing signals even
when “off,” many can send out your precise GPS location
whether you wish or not, and some models can be switched on remotely
as listening devices.  Users can't fix these malicious features
because they don't have control.

Some proprietary software is 
designed to restrict and attack its users.
Windows Vista was a big
advance in this field; the reason it required replacement of old
hardware is that the new models were designed to support unbreakable
restrictions.  Microsoft thus required users to pay for shiny new
shackles.  Vista was also designed to permit forced updating by corporate
authority.  Hence the Bad Vista
campaign, which urged Windows users not to “upgrade” to
Vista.  For later Windows versions, which are even more malicious, we
now have Upgrade from Windows.
Mac OS also contains features designed to restrict its users.

In 1999, Microsoft installed back doors for the US government's use.
Researchers 
disagree on what those back doors can 
do, but Microsoft has made that question less important by its forced 
software installation, which is even worse. If the 1999 code won't let 
NSA spy on you, Microsoft can force another change which will do so. 
Other proprietary programs may or may not have back doors, but since we 
cannot check them, we cannot trust them.

The only way to assure that your software is working for you is to
insist on free/libre software.  This means users get the source code,
are free to study and change it, and are free to redistribute it with
or without changes.  The GNU/Linux
system, developed specifically for users'
freedom, includes office applications, multimedia, games, and
everything you really need to run a computer.
See our list of totally free/libre
versions of GNU/Linux.

A special problem occurs when activists for social change use
proprietary software, because its developers, who control it, may be
companies they wish to protest—or that work hand in glove with the
states whose policies they oppose.  Control of our software by a
proprietary software company, whether it be Microsoft, Apple, Adobe or
Skype, means control of what we can say, and to whom.  This threatens
our freedom in all areas of life.

There is also danger in using a company's server to do your word
processing or email—and not just if you are in China, as US lawyer
Michael Springmann discovered.  In 2003, AOL not only handed over to
the police his confidential discussions with clients, it also made his
email and his address list disappear, and didn't admit this was
intentional until one of its staff made a slip.  Springmann gave up on
getting his data back.

The US is not the only state that doesn't respect human rights, so
keep your data on your own computer, and your backups under your own
custody—and run your computer with free/libre software.
